core_summary:
Chapter Overview & Pedagogical Purpose:
This chapter provides a thorough experimental study of magnetic properties, magnetic vs. non-magnetic materials, magnetic poles, directive properties, and magnetic induction. Students discover that magnets attract specific materials like iron and steel while having no effect on wood, rubber, or plastic. It details magnetic force concentration at the North and South poles, how a freely suspended magnet points North-South, the construction of a magnetic compass, and safety precautions to prevent demagnetization.
This chapter investigates magnetic properties, magnetic vs. non-magnetic classification, magnetic poles, the directive property of freely suspended magnets, construction of magnetic compasses, single-touch magnetisation, and rules of magnetic attraction/repulsion. It details how magnetic attraction concentrates at the North (N) and South (S) poles and warns against physical damage (heating, hammering, dropping) that leads to demagnetization.

Detailed Section Breakdown & Curriculum Progression:
• 4.1 Magnetic and Non-magnetic Materials:
  Materials attracted by magnets are magnetic (iron, steel, nickel, cobalt). Materials not attracted are non-magnetic (wood, plastic, glass, rubber, copper, aluminum).
• 4.2 Magnetic Poles and Force Distribution:
  Every magnet possesses two poles: North Pole (N) and South Pole (S). Magnetic attraction is strongest at the poles and weakest at the middle. Magnetic poles always exist in inseparable pairs.
  Margin Insights: [Did You Know?: History of Navigation - Ancient Indian navigators used a magnetic device called 'Matsya-yantra' (iron fish floating in oil) to locate directional north at sea.]
• 4.3 Directive Property and Magnetic Compass:
  A freely suspended bar magnet always aligns itself in the geographic North-South direction. A magnetic compass utilizes a pivoted magnetic needle inside a dial with cardinal directions (N, S, E, W).
• 4.4 Single-Touch Magnetisation Method:
  An unmagnetized iron piece (like a sewing needle) can be converted into a temporary magnet by stroking it repeatedly (30-40 times) in one direction using one fixed pole of a bar magnet.
• 4.5 Magnetic Interaction Rules and Care of Magnets:
  Like poles repel each other (N repels N, S repels S); opposite poles attract each other (N attracts S). Magnets lose magnetism if heated, hammered, or dropped from heights.
  Margin Insights: [Precaution: Magnet Storage - Store bar magnets in pairs with opposite poles alongside each other, separated by a wooden piece, with soft iron keepers across the ends.]

Key Curricular Topics Covered:
• 4.1 Magnetic and Non-magnetic Materials - Testing everyday items with bar magnets.
• 4.2 Poles of a Magnet - Concentration of magnetic attraction at ends.
• 4.3 Finding Directions - Magnetic compass and freely suspended bar magnets.
• 4.4 Making Your Own Magnet - Single-touch magnetisation method.
• 4.5 Magnetic Interactions - Like poles repel, opposite poles attract.
• 4.6 Care and Storage of Magnets - Avoiding heat, hammering, and dropping.

Key Practical Activities & Investigative Guidelines:
• Activity  (): Objective: . Procedure: Place the iron needle flat on a table. -> Hold one pole of a bar magnet at one end of the needle and stroke along its length to the other end. -> Lift the magnet clear and return to the starting end. Repeat this single-direction stroking 30–40 times. -> Insert the magnetized needle horizontally through a cork piece floating in a bowl of water.. Key Observation: . Conclusion: Iron objects can be magnetized by single-touch stroking and exhibit directive properties when freely suspended..

Real-World Applications, Heritage Context & Cross-Disciplinary Connections:
• : Do not heat, drop, or hammer magnets! They lose their magnetic properties when subjected to harsh physical impact or heat.

key_concepts: Magnetic vs. Non-magnetic Substances (4.1 Classification of Materials): Magnetic Materials: Substances strongly attracted by magnets (iron, steel, nickel, cobalt). Non-magnetic Materials: Substances not attracted by magnets (wood, plastic, glass, rubber, copper, aluminum). (Real-World Example/Activity: Testing classroom objects (keys, pencils, erasers, clips) with a bar magnet) [Key Terms: Magnetic Material, Non-magnetic Material, Ferromagnetic]

Poles of a Magnet (4.2 Magnetic Poles and Force Distribution): Magnetic attraction is concentrated at two ends called North Pole (N) and South Pole (S). Magnetic force is weakest at the center of a bar magnet. Magnetic poles always exist in inseparable pairs. (Real-World Example/Activity: Rolling a bar magnet in a heap of steel paperclips; maximum clips stick at the two ends) [Key Terms: North Pole, South Pole, Pole Concentration]

Freely Suspended Alignment (4.3 Directive Property and Navigation): A freely suspended bar magnet always aligns itself along the geographic North-South direction. Magnetic Compass: A pivoted magnetized needle inside a dial marked with cardinal directions (N, S, E, W). Historical navigation: Early Indian sailors used the 'Matsya-yantra' (floating magnetic iron fish). (Real-World Example/Activity: Suspending a bar magnet using a thread and observing its resting direction) [Key Terms: Directive Property, Magnetic Compass, Matsya-yantra]

Making Artificial Magnets (4.4 Single-Touch Magnetisation): An unmagnetized iron piece (e.g., sewing needle) can be magnetized by stroking it repeatedly (30-40 times) in one direction using one fixed pole of a bar magnet. (Real-World Example/Activity: Stroking an iron needle with a bar magnet and floating it on a cork in water to act as a compass) [Key Terms: Single-Touch Method, Induced Magnetism]

Attraction, Repulsion, and Maintenance (4.5 Laws of Magnetism and Care of Magnets): Like poles repel each other (N-N repels, S-S repels). Opposite poles attract each other (N-S attracts). Repulsion is the only conclusive test for magnetism. Demagnetization occurs due to heating, hammering, dropping, or improper storage. (Real-World Example/Activity: Bringing two bar magnets close on toy cars; observing attraction vs push-back repulsion Storing magnets in pairs with opposite poles separated by wood and soft iron keepers) [Key Terms: Repulsion Test, Like Poles, Unlike Poles, Demagnetization, Iron Keepers]
Poles of a Magnet: Magnetic force is concentrated at the North and South poles and weakest at the center.
Directive Property: A freely suspended magnet aligns along Earth's North-South magnetic axis.
Laws of Magnetism: Like poles repel; unlike poles attract. Repulsion is the only sure test for magnetism.
Demagnetization: Magnets lose strength when heated, hammered, dropped, or improperly stored.

key_terms.definition: Materials that are attracted towards a magnet. (e.g., Iron, steel paperclips, nickel, cobalt.)
Materials that are not attracted by a magnet. (e.g., Wood, plastic, eraser rubber, glass.)
The two regions near the ends of a magnet where magnetic force is concentrated. (e.g., North Pole (N) and South Pole (S).)
A directional instrument containing a magnetized needle pivoted freely inside a dial marked with cardinal directions.
The only sure test for magnetism, as repulsion occurs exclusively between like poles of two magnets. (e.g., Bringing North pole near North pole causes them to push away.)
An ancient Indian directional navigation device consisting of a magnetized iron fish floating in oil.

key_takeaways: Magnetic poles always exist in inseparable pairs (N and S).
Repulsion between two objects confirms that both objects are magnetized.
Proper handling and soft iron keepers protect magnets from losing their magnetism over time.
